Weathering steel / FEA / fabrication

Corten Balustrade

Curved terrace balustrade. Designed it, checked it with FEA, fabricated it from box section, then left it outside to rust on purpose.

Architecture, structural judgement, and a lot of repetitive welding. A bought-in railing would have taken an afternoon.

See the FEA Watch fabrication
BUILD SPEC 65 POSTS / 13M
Material
6mm corten plate, guillotined to size by a supplier in Sheffield. Corten is hard enough that I could not drill the fixing holes myself, so a local firm did those.
Sections
65 posts, each a 100 x 100mm box welded up from the flat plate, 1000mm tall and about 1.1m standing once the base is counted. Roughly 90mm of daylight between them.
Welding process
TIG, with a weathering-grade filler so the welds rust at the same rate as everything else. Standard wire would have left a pale line down the run forever.
Design check
FEA on the post and its base before anything was cut. Modelled in Fusion 360, which I would not use again — FreeCAD is king.
Run length
13m along the terrace, two bends at 10m radius each. Each post sits over three stainless threaded bars resined into the concrete beam, levelled on nuts.
Build time
A marathon: six evenings, ten posts a sitting. A day to drill and resin the threaded bar, then a few hours to hang and level the lot.

What the FEA actually said

Under the design load the posts deflect a few millimetres in the direction that matters, which is what you want to know before cutting 65 of anything. Sideways the numbers were far larger, which does not matter because nothing pushes them that way. The thing the model did not tell me was whether a row of 65 posts at 90mm spacing would whistle in the wind. It does not. That was luck.

What I would change

Nothing about the balustrade — it does the job and it looks right. I would model the airflow, though, rather than find out about whistling by standing on the terrace in a gale and listening. It took two years to start looking good and seven to look like it had always been there, which is the deal you make with weathering steel.

Cutting

Welding

From box section to balustrade.

The constraint

A curved edge is not a straight problem

The wall curves, so the balustrade had to follow it without looking fussy. Repeated verticals make the curve readable. The rust softens it against the fields.

Simulation

Analysis, then sparks

Model the loads, make the parts, check the fit, weld it up. Then the weather does the last finishing pass. Corten is the only material I have used where rusting is the plan.

Domestic fabrication

Fabricating in a half-built house

Some of it was welded on a table in the unfinished kitchen. Very on-brand for this house build. Dinner in the background, steel on the table, tools everywhere.

In use

It became part of the place.

My favourite photos are not the fabrication ones. They are the ones with people leaning on it, talking, looking at the fields.
